title: The rules that make approval automatic
question: Which ordinances since 2018 moved an approval from the Board to staff, raised a line below which no vote is needed, or let something take effect unless someone objects?
finding: Of 2,367 ordinances passed since 2018, 99 do one of these things by their own titles: removes a hearing, notice or permit step (53); hands the Board’s own approval to an official (16); lets a department approve or sign on its own (11); sets competition or contracting rules aside (11); raises a dollar line (5); takes effect or renews by itself (3). 35 delegate, raise a line or take effect by default; 13 of those passed in 2018 to 2021 and 19 in 2023 to 2026. Three passed in the last two years bear directly on money: ordinance 010-25 (12 February 2025) lets the Mayor approve certain contracts, grants and leases for homelessness and related work if the Board has not acted within 45 days; ordinance 135-26 (23 July 2026) raises the line for a Board vote on accepting a grant from $100,000 to $1,000,000; ordinance 205-26 (2 October 2026) raises the City Attorney’s authority to settle claims from $25,000 to $100,000. Voters then raised the contract line itself on 3 November 2026.
how: Every ordinance passed from January 2018 to November 2026, from the Board’s own records, is tested by the wording of its short and long titles against six patterns, first match winning, in the order shown. “In its own words” is the clause of the long title that matched, cut to 25 words. Rules that delegate, raise a line or take effect by default are listed first, newest first; then those that set competition aside or remove a hearing or permit step. The last column marks ordinances that are also in the project’s index of permit and fee rules.
limits: Each of these was itself voted on in public, and the titles point to the reasons: housing production, small-business permits, services for homeless people, and keeping dollar thresholds in step with consumer prices. Raising a line to keep pace with prices is routine. The sorting is by title wording: a title that mentions a threshold may lower it, and one that delegates may add a reporting duty in the same breath; read the clause quoted and the file. Ordinances whose titles do not use these words are missed. The count shows direction, not effect: how much money each rule moved out of view is measured in the other screens where the records allow. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
